::: {.solutions}

The official Notes say it plainly: *"Almost every TMUA paper will have some questions based on the terms
necessary and sufficient."* Count them and you find the same — seven appearances in 2019, ten in 2021,
eight in each of 2022 and 2023. **This is the most-tested pair of words on Paper 2.**

They are also two words you already understand, wearing new clothes. *Sufficient* is the arrow you have
been drawing since Session 1; *necessary* is that arrow **turned round** — which means it is the
**converse**, and everything Session 2 taught you about converses applies here.

::: {.callout-important}
## The two lines this whole session rests on

$$\textbf{“}A \textbf{ is sufficient for } B \textbf{”} \;=\; A \Rightarrow B \qquad\qquad
\textbf{“}A \textbf{ is necessary for } B \textbf{”} \;=\; B \Rightarrow A$$

**Sufficient points forwards. Necessary points backwards.** Everything else on this page is practice at
applying those two lines quickly, under wording designed to disguise them.
:::

Specification: **Arg2** — *understand and use the terms necessary and sufficient.*
Official source: **Notes on Logic and Proof**, pp. 51–55.

---

# Part 1 — Easy

## Question 1

::: {.question}
$P$ and $Q$ are statements. Write each of the following as an implication.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $P$ is **sufficient** for $Q$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) $P$ is **necessary** for $Q$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) $Q$ is **sufficient** for $P$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) $P$ is **necessary and sufficient** for $Q$. **[1]**
:::

Work strictly by the two lines in the box above, and [do not reason about what the words feel like]{.hl}
— *necessary* sounds stronger than *sufficient* in everyday English, and that intuition is exactly what
makes people draw the arrow the wrong way. Notice that (b) and (c) should come out identical, which is a
useful check that you applied the rules rather than your instincts.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — translating *sufficient* and *necessary* into arrows
:::


**(a)** $P \Rightarrow Q$ &nbsp; — *sufficient points forwards.*

**(b)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp; — *necessary points backwards.*

**(c)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp; — *sufficient again, but with the letters swapped, so the arrow starts
at $Q$.*

**(d)** $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ &nbsp; — *both directions at once.*

$\blacksquare$

As predicted, **(b) and (c) are the same implication**. So *"$P$ is necessary for $Q$"* and *"$Q$ is
sufficient for $P$"* say exactly the same thing — two sentences that look nothing alike in English.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (b) written as $P \Rightarrow Q$ | The commonest error in this topic. **Necessary reverses the arrow.** |
| Treating "necessary" as the stronger word | Neither is stronger — they point in **opposite directions**. A condition can be necessary without being sufficient, and vice versa. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the official summary table

The Notes give this table, and it is worth knowing in both directions:

| Phrase | Same as | Arrow |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ is **sufficient** for $B$ | *$A$ only if $B$*, *if $A$ then $B$* | $A \Rightarrow B$ |
| $A$ is **necessary** for $B$ | *$A$ if $B$*, *if $B$ then $A$* | $B \Rightarrow A$ |
| $A$ is **necessary and sufficient** for $B$ | *$A$ if and only if $B$* | $A \Leftrightarrow B$ |

**How to remember which way each points.**

- **Sufficient** = *enough on its own*. If $A$ is enough to guarantee $B$, then having $A$ **gets you**
  $B$: $A \Rightarrow B$.
- **Necessary** = *cannot do without*. If $B$ cannot happen without $A$, then whenever you find $B$ you
  must already have had $A$: $B \Rightarrow A$.

**The picture** (the Notes use it too). Read $A \Rightarrow B$ as "circle $A$ inside circle $B$".

- **$A$ sufficient for $B$:** $A$ sits **inside** $B$. Landing in $A$ guarantees you are in $B$.
- **$A$ necessary for $B$:** $B$ sits **inside** $A$. You must be inside $A$ to have any chance of being
  in $B$ — but being in $A$ is **not enough**, since $A$ is the bigger region.

That last sentence is the heart of it: *necessary* means you cannot manage without it, **not** that it
suffices.
:::

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.6))

# --- sufficient: A inside B
ax = axes[0]
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), 2.6, fc=YINT_CLR, alpha=0.10, ec=YINT_CLR, lw=2))
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((-0.5, -0.2), 1.25, fc=ROOT_CLR, alpha=0.22, ec=ROOT_CLR, lw=2))
ax.text(-0.5, -0.25, '$A$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, color=ROOT_CLR)
ax.text(1.5, 1.7, '$B$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, color=YINT_CLR)
ax.set_title('$A$ is SUFFICIENT for $B$\n$A\\Rightarrow B$ — being in $A$ guarantees $B$', fontsize=11)

# --- necessary: B inside A
ax = axes[1]
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), 2.6, fc=ROOT_CLR, alpha=0.14, ec=ROOT_CLR, lw=2))
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((-0.5, -0.2), 1.25, fc=YINT_CLR, alpha=0.18, ec=YINT_CLR, lw=2))
ax.text(-0.5, -0.25, '$B$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, color=YINT_CLR)
ax.text(1.5, 1.7, '$A$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, color=ROOT_CLR)
ax.plot([1.5], [-1.1], 'o', color=ASYM_CLR, ms=9, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('in $A$ but not in $B$:\n$A$ was needed,\nbut is NOT enough',
            (1.5, -1.1), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-30, -58), fontsize=9, color=ASYM_CLR,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=ASYM_CLR, lw=1.2))
ax.set_title('$A$ is NECESSARY for $B$\n$B\\Rightarrow A$ — no $B$ without $A$', fontsize=11)

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlim(-3.2, 3.6); ax.set_ylim(-4.0, 3.2)
    ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Let $n$ be a positive integer. For each pair of conditions, state whether the first is **sufficient**,
**necessary**, **both**, or **neither** for the second.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) "$n$ is divisible by $4$" &nbsp;·&nbsp; "$n$ is even" **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) "$n$ is even" &nbsp;·&nbsp; "$n$ is divisible by $4$" **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) "$n$ is divisible by $2$ and by $3$" &nbsp;·&nbsp; "$n$ is divisible by $6$" **[2]**
:::

For each pair, [test the two arrows separately]{.hl} — ask "does the first force the second?" and then
"does the second force the first?" — and answer each with a proof or a counterexample. Parts (a) and (b)
are deliberately the same two conditions in the opposite order, so if your answers to them are not
mirror images of each other, something has gone wrong.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — deciding necessity and sufficiency in a concrete case
:::


**(a) Sufficient, but not necessary.**

- Forwards: if $4$ divides $n$ then $n = 4k = 2(2k)$, so $n$ is even. ✓ So it **is sufficient**.
- Backwards: $n = 2$ is even but not divisible by $4$. ✗ So it is **not necessary**.

**(b) Necessary, but not sufficient.** *(The mirror image of (a), as it must be.)*

- "Even" is forced by "divisible by $4$", so evenness is **necessary**. ✓
- But $n=2$ is even without being divisible by $4$, so evenness is **not sufficient**. ✗

**(c) Both** — necessary and sufficient.

- Forwards: if $2$ divides $n$ and $3$ divides $n$, then since $2$ and $3$ share no common factor, $6$ divides $n$. ✓
- Backwards: if $6$ divides $n$ then $n = 6k = 2(3k) = 3(2k)$, so $2$ divides $n$ and $3$ divides $n$. ✓

$\blacksquare$

Notice the pattern in (a) and (b): [swapping the order of the two conditions swaps *sufficient* and
*necessary*]{.hl}. That is just the two lines from the top of the page, seen from the other end.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Answering (a) and (b) the same way | They are opposite questions. "$X$ sufficient for $Y$" and "$Y$ sufficient for $X$" are different claims. |
| Claiming "necessary" in (a) without testing backwards | Necessity needs the **backwards** arrow, and $n=2$ kills it. |
| Answering "neither" whenever a counterexample appears | A counterexample kills **one** direction. Check the other before concluding. |
:::

Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the four possible verdicts

Given two conditions $A$ and $B$, there are exactly four answers, and you settle it by testing **two
arrows**:

| $A \Rightarrow B$? | $B \Rightarrow A$? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| ✓ | ✗ | $A$ is **sufficient but not necessary** for $B$ |
| ✗ | ✓ | $A$ is **necessary but not sufficient** for $B$ |
| ✓ | ✓ | $A$ is **necessary and sufficient** for $B$ (they are equivalent) |
| ✗ | ✗ | **neither** |

**The method, every time.**

1. Test $A \Rightarrow B$: prove it, or find a counterexample.
2. Test $B \Rightarrow A$: prove it, or find a counterexample.
3. Read the verdict off the table.

**A useful way to feel it.** A *sufficient* condition is **strong** — it may ask for more than is
required, but it certainly delivers. A *necessary* condition is **weak** — it must hold, but it may not
be enough on its own.

- "Divisible by $4$" is **stronger** than "even": strong enough to guarantee evenness, so *sufficient*.
- "Even" is **weaker** than "divisible by $4$": implied by it but not enough to give it, so *necessary*.

Whenever one condition is genuinely stronger than the other, the stronger one is **sufficient** for the
weaker, and the weaker one is **necessary** for the stronger.
:::

# Part 2 — Medium

## Question 3

::: {.question}
Write each of the following as an implication between $P$ and $Q$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) A **sufficient** condition for $Q$ is $P$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) A **necessary** condition for $Q$ is $P$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) $P$ is a **necessary** condition for $Q$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) For $Q$ to hold it is **sufficient** that $P$ holds. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(e) For $Q$ to hold it is **necessary** that $P$ holds. **[1]**
:::

This is the wording the TMUA actually uses, and it is **written back to front on purpose**: the target
comes first and the condition second, so the sentence reads in the opposite order to the arrow you will
draw. The safe routine is to [find the two statements, decide which one is the *condition* and which is
the *target*, and only then apply the rule]{.hl} — never translate left-to-right.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — the reversed wording: *"a sufficient condition for … is …"*
:::


In every part, $P$ is **the condition** and $Q$ is **the target** — that is what the phrase "*condition
for $Q$*" tells you.

**(a)** $P \Rightarrow Q$ &nbsp; — *$P$ is sufficient, so $P$ delivers $Q$.*

**(b)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp; — *$P$ is necessary, so $Q$ cannot happen without $P$.*

**(c)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp; — *the same as (b); only the word order changed.*

**(d)** $P \Rightarrow Q$ &nbsp; — *"sufficient that $P$" = $P$ is enough.*

**(e)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp; — *"necessary that $P$" = no $Q$ without $P$.*

$\blacksquare$

So there are really only two answers here, dressed five ways: **sufficient gives $P \Rightarrow Q$, and
necessary gives $Q \Rightarrow P$**, no matter how the sentence is arranged.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Reading (a) left to right as $Q \Rightarrow P$ | The sentence names the **target first**. Identify condition and target before drawing anything. |
| Thinking (b) and (c) differ | Identical in meaning. English lets you put the condition either side of "is". |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — a routine for the reversed wording

Every sentence of this type contains a **condition** and a **target**. The word *"for"* points at the
target:

$$\text{a } \underbrace{\text{sufficient}}_{\text{which rule}} \text{ condition } \underbrace{\text{for } Q}_{\text{TARGET}} \text{ is } \underbrace{P}_{\text{CONDITION}}$$

**Three steps.**

1. **Find the target** — it follows the word *for*.
2. **Find the condition** — it is the other statement.
3. **Apply the rule**, always in terms of condition and target:
   - **sufficient** &nbsp;$\longrightarrow$&nbsp; condition $\Rightarrow$ target
   - **necessary** &nbsp;$\longrightarrow$&nbsp; target $\Rightarrow$ condition

Written that way, the rule never changes even though the English word order does.

**Worth recognising**, because the exam mixes them freely — all of these say $P \Rightarrow Q$:

- $P$ is sufficient for $Q$
- a sufficient condition for $Q$ is $P$
- for $Q$ it is sufficient that $P$
- $P$ only if $Q$
- if $P$ then $Q$
- $Q$ if $P$
- $Q$ is necessary for $P$ &nbsp;← *watch this one: necessary, but the letters are swapped*

That last line is the sting: **"$Q$ is necessary for $P$" and "$P$ is sufficient for $Q$" are the same
statement.** Both are $P \Rightarrow Q$.
:::

## Question 4

::: {.question}
Let $ABC$ and $DEF$ be triangles.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Explain why "the two triangles have an angle in common" is a **necessary** condition for
them to be similar. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Show that it is **not sufficient**. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) State a condition that **is** sufficient for the triangles to be similar. **[1]**
:::

Part (b) is the one that carries the marks, and it asks for something very specific: to show a condition
is *not* sufficient you must [produce a case where the condition holds and the conclusion fails]{.hl} —
a counterexample, not an explanation. This is exactly the "one forbidden combination" from Session 2,
used deliberately.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — *necessary but not sufficient*, and how to demonstrate it
:::


**(a)** If two triangles are similar, then all three of their angles are equal in pairs — so in
particular they have an angle in common. That is the implication

$$(\text{similar}) \Rightarrow (\text{share an angle}) ,$$

and a condition implied *by* the target is precisely what **necessary** means. ✓

**(b)** We need a case where the condition **holds** but similarity **fails**. Take

- triangle $1$ with angles $90^\circ, 60^\circ, 30^\circ$;
- triangle $2$ with angles $90^\circ, 45^\circ, 45^\circ$.

Both contain a $90^\circ$ angle, so they share an angle — yet their remaining angles differ, so they are
**not** similar. The condition therefore does not guarantee similarity: it is **not sufficient**. ✓

**(c)** Several work. The three standard tests for **similarity** are:

- **all three angles equal** (equivalently, two angles equal — the third follows) &nbsp;*(AA)*;
- **all three pairs of sides in the same ratio** &nbsp;*(SSS)*;
- **two pairs of sides in the same ratio with the included angle equal** &nbsp;*(SAS)*.

$\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Similar is not the same as congruent — mind the wording.** Similarity is about **shape**, so its side
conditions say *"in the same **ratio**"*. Congruence is about **shape *and* size**, so its side
conditions say the sides are *"**equal**"*. Writing "all three sides **equal**" as a condition for
*similarity* is over-strong — that is the test for *congruence*.

In fact this is itself a necessary/sufficient statement, and a clean one:
$$\text{congruent} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{similar} \qquad \text{but} \qquad \text{similar} \;\not\Rightarrow\; \text{congruent}.$$
So **being congruent is sufficient for being similar, but not necessary** — two triangles can be similar
(same shape) without being congruent (a small one and a large one). Congruence is just similarity with
ratio $1$.
:::

*Notice how the answer to (c) is a **stronger** condition than the one in (a) — strong enough to
deliver similarity, where sharing a single angle was not.*

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Answering (b) with an explanation instead of an example | *"Sharing one angle doesn't tell you about the others"* is the right idea but earns little. **Produce two specific triangles.** |
| Giving a counterexample where the triangles are not similar **and** share no angle | Useless — the condition must **hold** in your example, or it tests nothing. |
| Writing "all three sides **equal**" as a condition for **similarity** | That is the *congruence* test. For similarity the sides are in the same **ratio**, not equal. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — proving each of the four verdicts

| To show … | You must produce |
|---|---|
| $A$ **is sufficient** for $B$ | a **proof** that $A \Rightarrow B$ |
| $A$ is **not** sufficient for $B$ | a **counterexample**: a case with $A$ true and $B$ false |
| $A$ **is necessary** for $B$ | a **proof** that $B \Rightarrow A$ |
| $A$ is **not** necessary for $B$ | a **counterexample**: a case with $B$ true and $A$ false |

**Read the two counterexample rows carefully — they are different cases**, and picking the wrong one is
a standard way to lose marks:

- to break **sufficiency**, your example must satisfy $A$ but fail $B$;
- to break **necessity**, your example must satisfy $B$ but fail $A$.

A single example almost never does both jobs, so decide which claim you are attacking before you start
hunting.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Where this shows up in real questions.** STEP and MAT questions often say *"show that … is a sufficient
condition but not a necessary condition for …"* — which is asking for **one proof and one
counterexample**, in that order. The Notes quote exactly such a question from STEP I 2001.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**A clean example to keep in mind: congruent vs similar triangles.**

- **Congruent** $\Rightarrow$ **similar** (same shape and size $\Rightarrow$ same shape). So congruence is
  a **sufficient** condition for similarity.
- **Similar** $\not\Rightarrow$ **congruent** (a photo enlargement is the same shape, not the same size).
  So congruence is **not necessary** for similarity.

The same relationship in every direction:

| Statement | True? | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Congruent is *sufficient* for similar | ✓ | congruent $\Rightarrow$ similar |
| Congruent is *necessary* for similar | ✗ | similar triangles need not be congruent |
| Similar is *necessary* for congruent | ✓ | congruent $\Rightarrow$ similar, so you can't be congruent without being similar |
| Similar is *sufficient* for congruent | ✗ | similar $\not\Rightarrow$ congruent |

Whenever one property is "the other plus something extra" — here, *plus equal size* — the **stronger** one
is sufficient for the weaker, and the weaker is necessary for the stronger.
:::
:::

# Part 3 — Hard

## Question 5

::: {.question}
$n$ is a positive integer. Consider the theorem

$$\text{If } n \text{ is a perfect square, then } n \text{ is not prime.} \tag{$*$}$$

Which of the following, **taken individually**, is/are equivalent to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; A sufficient condition for $n$ not to be prime is that $n$ is a perfect square.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $n$ being a perfect square is necessary for $n$ not to be prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; If $n$ is prime, then $n$ is not a perfect square.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** II only &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** III only &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** I and II &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** I and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** II and III &nbsp;&nbsp;
**G** I, II and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** None
:::

Name the halves and write $(*)$ as one arrow before you read the options. Then classify each of I, II,
III — one is the original restyled, one is the contrapositive, and one is the converse. Be careful with
II: [it uses *necessary*, so the arrow it produces runs the other way]{.hl}, however natural the sentence
sounds.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — sorting rephrasings, at exam speed
:::


Let $P$ = "$n$ is a perfect square" and $Q$ = "$n$ is not prime". Then $(*) = P \Rightarrow Q$.

**I.** "A **sufficient** condition **for $Q$** is $P$" — target $Q$, condition $P$, rule *sufficient*, so
$$P \Rightarrow Q .$$
That is $(*)$ itself. **Equivalent.** ✓

**II.** "$P$ is **necessary** for $Q$" — *necessary* reverses, so
$$Q \Rightarrow P .$$
That is the **converse**. **Not equivalent.** ✗

*(It is also false: $n = 6$ is not prime and not a perfect square.)*

**III.** "If $n$ is prime, then $n$ is not a perfect square" is
$$\text{not } Q \Rightarrow \text{not } P ,$$
negated **and** reversed — the **contrapositive**. **Equivalent.** ✓

**Answer: E (I and III).** $\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Reading I backwards because the target is written first | *"condition **for** $Q$"* names the target. The condition is $P$, and *sufficient* sends it forwards. |
| Accepting II because it sounds like a restatement | *Necessary* always reverses the arrow. Here that turns $(*)$ into its converse. |
| Missing III because of the double negatives | Both halves negated **and** swapped is the contrapositive — always equivalent, however awkward it reads. |
:::

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the complete translation table

By now every phrase you will meet on Paper 2 reduces to one of three arrows. This is the whole of
Sessions 1–3 on one card:

| $P \Rightarrow Q$ | $Q \Rightarrow P$ | $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ |
|---|---|---|
| if $P$ then $Q$ | if $Q$ then $P$ | $P$ if and only if $Q$ |
| $P$ only if $Q$ | $P$ if $Q$ | $P$ iff $Q$ |
| $Q$ if $P$ | $Q$ only if $P$ | $P$ is necessary and sufficient for $Q$ |
| $P$ is sufficient for $Q$ | $P$ is necessary for $Q$ | $P$ and $Q$ are equivalent |
| $Q$ is necessary for $P$ | $Q$ is sufficient for $P$ | |
| a sufficient condition for $Q$ is $P$ | a necessary condition for $Q$ is $P$ | |
| not $Q \Rightarrow$ not $P$ *(contrapositive)* | not $P \Rightarrow$ not $Q$ *(inverse)* | |

**Reading the table.** Anything in the **same column** is the same statement. Anything in a **different
column** is not — no matter how similar the English looks.

The two columns on the left are converses of each other, which is why *sufficient* and *necessary* land
in different columns, and why *necessary* is where the marks are lost.
:::

---

## Question 6

::: {.question}
Let $x$ be a real number, and consider the target statement $T$: &nbsp; $x^2 > 4$.

For each condition below, state whether it is **sufficient**, **necessary**, **both**, or **neither**
for $T$, justifying each answer with a proof or a counterexample.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $x > 2$ **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) $|x| > 2$ **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) $x > 1$ **[2]**
:::

Each part needs **both** arrows tested, so six checks in all — and [a counterexample for one direction
says nothing about the other]{.hl}. Before starting, note that $x^2 > 4$ means $|x| > 2$, that is,
$x > 2$ **or** $x < -2$; keeping that description in view makes every part quick.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — comparing the strength of several conditions
:::


First rewrite the target: $\;x^2 > 4 \iff |x| > 2 \iff (x > 2 \text{ or } x < -2)$.

**(a) $x > 2$: sufficient, but not necessary.**

- Forwards: if $x > 2$ then $x^2 > 4$. ✓
- Backwards: $x = -3$ gives $x^2 = 9 > 4$, but $x \not> 2$. ✗

*The negative branch is what breaks necessity — a recurring theme whenever squares are involved.*

**(b) $|x| > 2$: both — necessary and sufficient.**

- It is exactly equivalent to $x^2 > 4$, as noted above. ✓✓

**(c) $x > 1$: neither.**

- Forwards: $x = 1.5$ gives $x^2 = 2.25 \not> 4$. ✗ Not sufficient.
- Backwards: $x = -3$ gives $x^2 = 9 > 4$ but $x \not> 1$. ✗ Not necessary.

$\blacksquare$

Line the three up and the structure is clear: (a) is **too strong** (it delivers the target but demands
more than needed), (c) is **too weak in one direction and too narrow in the other**, and only (b)
matches the target exactly.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (a) called "both" | It fails backwards. Always test the negative values of $x$ when squares appear. |
| (c) called "necessary" because $x^2>4$ often has $x>1$ | *Often* is not *always*: $x=-3$ satisfies the target and fails the condition. |
| Using one counterexample for both directions | They are different tests, and generally need different examples. |
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — strength, and how conditions relate

Think of each condition as a **set of $x$ values**, and the target as another set. Then:

| Relationship of sets | Verdict |
|---|---|
| condition **inside** target | **sufficient** (enough, possibly more than needed) |
| condition **contains** target | **necessary** (implied, but too broad to guarantee) |
| the sets **coincide** | **necessary and sufficient** |
| the sets **overlap partially** | **neither** |

In Question 6 with target $\{x : x<-2 \text{ or } x>2\}$:

- (a) $\{x>2\}$ is a **subset** — inside, so sufficient only.
- (b) $\{|x|>2\}$ is the **same set** — so both.
- (c) $\{x>1\}$ **overlaps** it (shares $x>2$, but includes $1<x\le2$ and misses $x<-2$) — so neither.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The squares warning.** Any time the target involves $x^2$, check the **negative** branch before
declaring necessity. It is the single most productive counterexample-hunting habit on Paper 2, and it
has now appeared in Sessions 1, 2 and 3.
:::
:::

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2, 3.4))
rows = [
    ('target:  $x^2>4$',      [(-6, -2), (2, 6)], ASYM_CLR),
    ('(a)  $x>2$',            [(2, 6)],           ROOT_CLR),
    ('(b)  $|x|>2$',          [(-6, -2), (2, 6)], YINT_CLR),
    ('(c)  $x>1$',            [(1, 6)],           '#7a5195'),
]
for i, (label, segs, c) in enumerate(rows):
    y = len(rows) - i
    for a, b in segs:
        ax.plot([a, b], [y, y], color=c, lw=7, solid_capstyle='butt', alpha=.85)
    ax.text(-6.4, y, label, ha='right', va='center', fontsize=10)

ax.axvline(-2, color='grey', ls='--', lw=1); ax.axvline(2, color='grey', ls='--', lw=1)
ax.axvline(1, color='grey', ls=':', lw=1)
ax.set_xticks([-6, -2, 0, 1, 2, 6]); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlim(-11, 6.4); ax.set_ylim(0.4, 4.6)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
ax.set_title('(a) sits inside the target → sufficient only.  (b) matches it → both.\n(c) overlaps → neither.',
             fontsize=11)
for s in ('top', 'right', 'left'): ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
